description: We are a team of 5 friends from Cal Poly Pomona building a space mission design game for the Space Apps Challenge. We bring a diverse mix of engineering, systems design, and life sciences to the table, allowing us to balance the technical physics of spaceflight with the realities of crew health. We love turning complex scientific concepts into engaging gameplay!
summary: Our Godot mission design game lets players plan and play space mission throuhg an interactive, hands-on experience. By connecting an Arduino Uno and joystick to the game, we give players a physical way to control their actions and explore the mission environment.
details:
For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, our five-member team, CTRL+ALT+BRONCOS, built Touch The Frontier, an interactive space mission design game. We wanted to combine our different backgrounds, spanning aerospace, biotechnology, and electrical engineering at Cal Poly Pomona, into something that bridged software simulation with a custom physical interface. The game lets players design and navigate space mission scenarios in Godot, but instead of just clicking around with a mouse, we built a physical analog joystick controller from scratch to make the experience much more immersive.

The hardware side runs on an Arduino Uno R3 wired to an analog joystick module. We wrote a C++ script for the microcontroller to read the analog voltage coordinates and button clicks, which then outputs a continuous binary data stream over USB. To get this talking to the Godot engine without triggering software-input blocks, we built an asynchronous Python bridge using the pyserial and pydirectinput libraries. This script translates the serial data into low-level DirectX hardware scan codes, essentially tricking the computer's operating system into registering our Arduino as a native, physical computer keyboard.

Getting the hardware and software to play nice together was easily the most creative and challenging part of the build. We originally attempted to use an ESP32 to create a wireless Bluetooth controller, but after fighting with severe compiler conflicts and bootloader timeouts, we had to pivot. We swapped to the hardwired Arduino setup for competition stability and engineered a custom 100-millisecond polling algorithm in Python to create a smooth, continuous turbo-fire movement effect in-game. The team had to constantly balance input latency with serial baud rates and buffer clearing to make sure the controls felt snappy and responsive rather than laggy.

Ultimately, the goal of the project is to make complex aerospace concepts way more approachable. Space mission planning can feel incredibly dry or intimidating when it is just math on a screen, but adding a tactile, physical controller completely changes the dynamic. It gamifies the learning process and lowers the barrier to entry, proving that you can take heavy simulation concepts and turn them into a hands-on, highly engaging experience for a broader audience.
